deck.topic: Texas transplant reality check: taxes, commutes, heat, schools, and what you get back
deck.hook: Transplants budget for month one. Month 14 is what breaks them.

points.title: Month Fourteen
body: Your first Texas tax bill often reflects the old owner's value, or a bare lot if the house was new.
Month 14 is when the county sends one based on what you actually paid.
That jump is the number nobody puts in their moving budget.

points.title: Miles Lie
body: Twelve miles in Austin at 8am is a different life than twelve miles at 10am.
In DFW people pay tolls daily just to buy back twenty minutes.
Ask for drive times, not distances, before you fall in love with a house.

points.title: The Summer Tax
body: June through September, outdoor life happens before nine and after eight.
San Antonio holds the heat longer than Austin does, and the electric bill follows.
Shade, orientation, and a working patio matter more here than square footage.

points.title: Ratings Are A Snapshot
body: Texas districts redraw attendance boundaries as new rooftops go up.
The campus you bought for can change while you still own the house.
Buy the district and the trend, not one number on an app.
points.loop: You get something back for this.

points.title: What You Get Back
body: No state income tax means your take home is bigger from the first paycheck.
A full Saturday out costs a fraction of what it did in California or Illinois.
Hill country, the coast, and lake weekends are all one tank of gas away.
points.loop: Most people run this too late.

linkedinCaption:
Most of the surprises new Texas homeowners hit are not in the listing. They show up in month fourteen, when the county reassesses at what you actually paid, or in traffic, where twelve miles at 8am is nothing like twelve miles at 10am.

I put together five things I wish more relocating buyers heard before they committed. Property tax timing. Drive times over distances. The summer utility reality and why orientation and shade matter more than square footage here. School boundaries that move as new rooftops go up. And the real offsets, including no state income tax and weekends that cost a fraction of what they did back home.

For those of you advising relocating clients, which of these catches people off guard most often?
